en: I take refuge in the primordial couple, whose two feet are ever-watchful in generating the manifold diversity of the world, and who are experts in the flavor of inseparable union.
I bow to the goddess Śāradā, the presiding deity of name and form, who possesses the nature of the essence of supreme joy and who is the moonlight for the night-lotus of reality.
The king of devotion, who is a bee at the lotus-feet of Śiva, rules over the earth—which yields abundant fruit and is girdled by the great ocean. || 3 ||
His son was the honored King Manma, the ornament of the lunar and solar dynasties, who bore the title Āgamamahāsamudra.
Once, in the midst of an assembly during the course of a poetic discussion,
he respectfully questioned Amṛtānanda, the lord of poets.

The purity of syllables, the poetic styles, the aesthetic flavors (rasas), the emotions (bhāvas) that follow them, the different types of protagonists, the ornaments (alaṅkāras), as well as the defects and their corresponding excellences (guṇas). || 6 ||
He [describes] the dramatic conventions, the divisions of dramas and minor dramas,
as well as the various types of panegyric compositions scattered here and there.
"Having reflected, relate it all in one place for the sake of the ease of the virtuous,"—thus requested by me, the yogin Amṛtānanda spoke as follows. (8)
Having carefully considered the meanings and various statements expressed in other tantras, this compendium of all poetic ornaments is properly composed. (9)
The phonemes beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa' constitute words;
words are of two kinds, distinguished by their endings in sup (nominal) or tiṅ (verbal) suffixes. || 10 ||
The wise call collections of nouns and verbs "sentences"; these very same [collections], when fashioned by poets, are meaningful and full of aesthetic flavor. (11)
The wise declare that poetry is that which is adorned with ornaments and free from defects;
it is said to be of three kinds: verse, prose, and mixed. || 12 ||

That which is composed in metrical verse is called *padya*, while prose is a collection of sentences; that which consists of both verse and prose is called mixed (*miśra*), such as the *nāṭaka* and other dramatic works. || 13 ||
A composition in cantos (sargabandha) written in Sanskrit, and one with narrative sections (sāśvāsa) in Prākṛt—
both of these constitute Mahākāvya, such as the Setubandha, the Rāmāyaṇa, and others.
Prose (gadya), however, is said to be of two kinds: the tale (kathā) and the narrative (ākhyāyikā).
A tale is considered to have a fictional account, while a narrative is held to have a true subject matter. || 15 ||
The chapter beginning with the "ucchvāsa-lambaka" is narrated in two prose sections;
it may be mixed [with verse] and provided with numerical divisions (aṅkas), and it is composed in many languages.
The introduction [to a literary work] consists of a benediction, a salutation, or a description of the subject matter;
it may also include descriptions of cities, oceans, mountains, seasons, and the rising of the moon and sun. (17)
Through descriptions of sporting in gardens and waters, festivals of delight in the drinking of honey-wine, separations, marriages, and the accounts of the rise of princes; || 18 ||

It is adorned with incantations, gambling, journeys, battles, and the triumphs of heroes; it is neither too concise nor lacking in the continuous flow of aesthetic flavor (rasa) and emotion (bhāva). (19)
Poetry, which depends on the fruits of the four aims of life and possesses four noble protagonists, is fashioned for the great welfare of beings and endures until the end of an aeon.
Metre (chandas) is pervaded by the *yagaṇa* and likewise by the *bha*, *ja*, and *sa* [gaṇas];
it is also pervaded by heavy (*guru*) and light (*laghu*) syllables; such is its definition. || 21 ||
The syllables ya, ra, ta, and sa attain lightness at the beginning, middle, and end;
the syllables bha and ja attain heaviness; but in the case of ma, there is both heaviness and lightness.
One should make the meter and the poetic style highly beautiful at the beginning of the poem;
by that means, prosperity arises for both the author and the hero. (23)
Otherwise, the attainment of undesirable results would occur for these two alone;
therefore, the purification of the letters and the groups [of consonants] should be understood in their proper sequence as follows. (24)

From these two, *mudī* vowels, there arises great joy and the acquisition of wealth; from the two *ṛ* vowels, there is ill-repute and loss. These [consonants] are considered to be bringers of happiness. (25)
A *bindu* (anusvāra) or a *sarga* (visarga) never occurs at the beginning of a word.

From the four letters beginning with *ka*, there is fortune; however, from the letter *ca*, there is infamy. From *cha*, there is affection and happiness; from *ja*, there is the acquisition of friends; and from *ña*, there is fear and death.
Jha and ṣṭa represent fatigue and suffering; ḍa and ḍha represent those who produce beauty and ugliness.
Wandering about brings no happiness; rather, it bestows the joy of battle. For our powerful [lord], fear produces neither pleasure nor the burning pain of death. (28)
The letter-group *pa* bestows fortune (*lakṣmī*), *ra* burns, *la* and *va* cause calamity;
*śa* extends happiness, *ṣa* causes distress, and *sa* is the giver of happiness. (29)
Ha causes burning; La brings misfortune; Kṣa bestows all prosperity. Thus has been declared the actual fruit of each of the letters individually.
Contact with others must be avoided by the castes in every way, except for the mouth;
even that which is pure becomes impure when joined with another. (31)
Just as honey mixed with ghee becomes poisonous by its potency,
so too should the fruit of the groups be understood, even as it is described for each individual.
The letter *va* is watery in nature and bestows wealth; *ra* is fire and causes fear of burning;
*ai* grants sovereignty; *na* is celestial and auspicious; *bha* is gentle and bestows happiness. || 33 ||
Ja is said to be the Sun, which bestows disease; So is Vāyavya, which grants happiness; Mo is Śubhada, consisting of Earth; and No is considered Gaur, which brings wealth. || 34 ||
Words that denote deities and those that denote auspicious things (such as *bhadra*) should never be censured, whether according to their spelling or their numerical class.
Thus, the pervasion of groups of phonemes is equal in both prose and verse; it should be understood by the best of the wise in Sanskrit, Prākṛta, and other languages. (36)

O Bhīma, whose lap is occupied by the young Kumāra, may your fame spread throughout the worlds through these prose and verse compositions— fresh, heart-stealing, and faultlessly crafted with words of certain and stainless beauty— inspiring wonder in the hearts of the learned.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "An Examination of Phonemes and Metrical Feet," in the *Alaṅkārasaṅgraha* composed by the lord of yogis, Amṛtānanda.
Thus, one who is skilled in investigating the pervasion of the collection of phonemes, and who is endowed with the multitude of factors that produce poetry, is called a poet (kavi). || 1 ||
The Raucika, the Vācika, the Ārtha, the Śilpaka, the Mārdavānuga, the Vivekī, and the Bhūṣaṇārthī—these are proclaimed as the seven types of poets. || 2 ||
He who effects the insertion and removal [of words] according to the pleasure of his own mind is a *raucika*; he who is verbal and produces a grand display of pure speech is a *vācika*. (3)
The *ārtha* (meaning-focused) poet seeks diverse meanings; the artisan (*śilpaka*) creates both [word and meaning] as his art;
the poet (*kavi*) should attend to the softness of word and meaning and follow that softness. || 4 ||

One who knows the words, meanings, merits, and defects; who follows the tradition of the great poets; who is refined by the study of the sciences and poetics; and who possesses discernment—such a person is a preeminent poet. || 5 ||
He who is solely devoted to ornamentation and seeks only embellishment is considered by the wise [to be a mere poet].
However, those who know the nature of poetry declare that creative power (*śakti*) is the primary cause of poetry. (6)
Proficiency in grammar, prosody, lexicography, and other sciences, as well as observation of the world, and poetic instruction—this triad is the cause of poetry. (7)
That power by which poetry is never produced even in the absence of causes such as vocabulary,
meter, and nomenclature is called *śakti*.
Even that which has been produced here serves only for the ridicule of the succession of poets;
for there is no rule here regarding the collection of words, meters, and designations.
Their specific nature should be understood from other sources by those possessed of intelligence;
the meanings of sentences composed by poets have been declared to be fourfold. (10)

In this context, it is said that [the meaning] is primary (mukhya), indicated (lakṣya), and likewise secondary (gauṇa) or suggested (vyaṅgya). That which is expressed directly through convention is called the primary [meaning]. (11)
That [denotative power] is also fourfold, based on the distinction between genus, action, quality, and substance;
"cow," "moving," "white," and "Ḍittha" are considered the examples. (12)

When the literal meaning is untenable, another related meaning is understood by virtue of a specific purpose; this indicated meaning (lakṣya-artha) is threefold, and this process is called indication (lakṣaṇā). (13)

Where another meaning is indicated through the abandonment of the literal meaning, that should be known as *jahat-lakṣaṇā* (indication with the exclusion of the primary sense), as in the example: "A hamlet on the Ganges. (14)
Where another meaning is indicated without the abandonment of the literal meaning, that is considered *ajahallakṣaṇā* (non-abandoning indication), as in "The spears enter. (15)
That which possesses both natures— both abandoning its own primary meaning and not abandoning it—
is considered to have "The men with umbrellas are walking" as its illustration.
In this world, the state of possessing umbrellas by others is indicated by a single person holding an umbrella;
that which is understood as another meaning due to similarity with a quality is called secondary (gauṇa). || 17 ||
An illustration of this is like the boy who is a lion;
when the primary meaning is obstructed, that which is suggested arises through its connection with the indicated meaning as the resulting fruit. (18)
This [meaning] is neither the primary sense nor the indicated sense, because it is the fruit of indication (lakṣaṇā).
In the case of "The Gaṅgā," the bank is the indicated sense, while coolness and so forth are the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya). || 19 ||
A word that possesses multiple denotative powers manifests its meaning within a sentence;
this manifestation, which is rooted in primary denotation (abhidhā), is said to arise from factors such as conjunction (saṃyoga) and so forth. (20)
Conjunction, disjunction, association, opposition, purpose, context, a characteristic mark, and the proximity of another word [are the factors that determine the specific meaning of a term]. || 21 ||
Capability, propriety, place, time, gender, accent, and so forth, are the causes for the recollection of specific meanings when the meaning of a word is otherwise undetermined. (22)
Indra is recognized through the application of the weapon-mantra "Savajro hariḥ" (the lion with the thunderbolt);
likewise, Vāsava is recognized even through the absence of the weapon-mantra "Avajro hariḥ" (the lion without the thunderbolt).
The term "son of Daśaratha" refers to both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa due to their constant association;
however, the term "Rāma who opposes Arjuna" is understood to refer to Bhārgava (Paraśurāma) because of his enmity [with Kārtavīryārjuna].
In the sense "Worship Sthāṇu, who is venerable by the world," Śiva is not intended;
rather, by virtue of the context, it means "The Lord knows me as one belonging to you. (25)
From the mark "the one whose banner is the fish," Kāma is understood;
in the phrase "the god who is the enemy of Pura," Śiva is [understood] from the proximity of the word.
"The cuckoo sings here because of me" implies, by the force of context, "in the spring season";
"May Śambhu protect you" is intended as a direct address due to propriety. (27)
In the expression "the king shines here," the king is understood through the location;
in "the sun shines," the object is determined by the time. (28)
If it occurs at night, it should be known as Anala; if by day, it is Tigmadīdhiti.
But Mitra shines as a friend; thus Bhāskara is he who shines as a friend. || 29 ||
These two are manifested respectively by the individual instances of the masculine and the neuter genders.
In the Veda, the meaning is manifested by the accent; in poetic compositions, it is never so.
When one possesses only this much capacity for vision, the object is discerned through its activity;
and in that case, the objects themselves are considered to be the manifestors by virtue of being auxiliary factors. || 31 ||
By the birds settling down, by the lotuses closing,
and by the jasmine flower blooming, it is known that the sun has set.
If the speaker here is the sacrificer, the time for the oblation is understood;
if it is a commoner (viṭ), it should be understood as the occasion of an attempt to approach a courtesan.
"Your flickering eyes are not able to move my mind"—in this sentence, the clarity of meaning is understood through the tone of voice (kāku). (34)
Such is their detailed exposition; it is not stated here in full.
Only a mere indication has been shown; let the wise understand what was left unsaid. (35)

May the sun of your majesty’s valor prevail—a sun marked by supreme, utterly unrestrained, and novel courage—through various distinctions in the application of speech and through the compositions of new poetry fashioned by the best of poets. 36.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Determination of Word and Meaning," in the *Alaṅkārasaṅgraha* composed by Amṛtānandayogīndra.
The sequence for the arising of knowledge is as follows: the union of the self with the mind, the mind with the senses, and the senses with their respective objects. (1)
The permanent emotion (sthāyin), manifested by the determinants (vibhāva) and other factors as they are being perceived, is known as rasa.
A bhāva, however, is a specific modification of the mind that has attained stability. (2)
Love, laughter, as well as sorrow, anger, energy, fear, as well as disgust, wonder, and tranquility—these are the nine permanent emotional states (sthāyibhāvas) in their respective order. (3)

The nine distinct varieties of aesthetic flavor (rasa) are, in their respective order: the erotic, the comic, the pathetic, the furious, the heroic, the terrible, the loathsome, the marvelous, and the peaceful. || 4 ||
When delight (rati) is nourished by various conditions (bhāvas), it is designated as the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra);
in this very same way, other permanent emotions (sthāyins) indeed attain the status of sentiments (rasas). || 5 ||
Just as fresh butter attains the state of clarified butter through cooking,
so too does the emergence of rasa occur in poems through the vibhāvas and other elements being heard.

In dramas, the emergence of aesthetic flavor (rasa) for the members of the assembly occurs through the visible determinants (vibhāvas), consequents (anubhāvas), involuntary states (sāttvikas), and transitory emotions (vyabhicārins). || 7 ||
For both the listeners and the spectators, all of these are nourishers of aesthetic flavor (rasa);
they are considered to be of two kinds: as the objective basis (ālambana) and as the excitant (uddīpana).
The manifestation of rasa is specifically cultivated through the determinants (vibhāvas) and other factors;
that which is relied upon for the emergence of rasa is the objective determinant (ālambana-vibhāva).
Those factors by which the rasa is kindled are considered the excitants (uddīpana);
those factors by which the rasa, once produced, is experienced through the various states (bhāvas) are the ensuants (anubhāvas).
These are proclaimed as the *anubhāvas*, while the *vibhāvas* arise from the limbs [of the body].
That which is called *sattva* is a function of the mind; the *sāttvikas* originate from that. (11)
Stupor, perspiration, horripilation, paralysis, change of voice, trembling, tears, and change of color—these eight states have been declared by the wise. (12)
While the stable emotion (sthāyin) remains constant, the transitory emotions (vyabhicārin) arise and dissolve due to their variability, like waves in the ocean. || 13 ||
Disgust, languor, apprehension, fatigue, fortitude, dullness, joy, dejection, intense anxiety,
fear, envy, resentment, pride, recollection, death, intoxication, sleep, slumber, awakening,
shame, epilepsy, delusion, equanimity, lassitude, impetuosity, deliberation, and dissimulation.
Disease, insanity, poison, longing, and fickleness—these thirty and three [make up the total]. 14.

Because the aesthetic emotions (rasa) and mental states (bhāva) are merely observed in actors and not present in reality, rasa exists only among the audience, due to their recollection of the rasas inherent in their own respective natures. (15)
In this world, for all living beings, there is a natural aesthetic flavor (*rasa*);
in the case of the flavor of love between a beloved woman and a lover, it consists of their mutual dependence upon one another.
In the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), the excitants (uddīpana) are moonlight, groves, and so forth;
the ensuants (anubhāva) are proclaimed to be side-long glances, casting [of looks], and so forth. || 17 ||

Stupefaction and the other *sāttvika* states occur during seeing, touching, and so forth; furthermore, the transitory (*sañcārī*) emotions, such as despondency and the rest, should be applied as appropriate. (18)

The erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) is considered to be of two kinds: union (sambhoga) and separation (viprayoga). Union is proximity [between lovers], such as through mutual conversation and the like. (19)
Your face is bowed, its eyes timid with shame; your hands tremble violently; your breasts, with their sunken navels, are touched and bristling with horripilation;
and your slender body is starred by a fine network of droplets from perspiration.
Existence is known through the royal fortune born of existence; enough with external displays of grandeur.
Separation (vipralambha) is of many kinds, such as that caused by longing, jealousy, or dwelling abroad;
examples of these will be described within the eight stages [of love].
Ten stages arising from the exhilaration of passion exist here:
visual delight, attachment of the mind, volition, and likewise wakefulness. (21)

The attenuation of aversion toward sense objects, followed by the destruction of shame, and then delusion, fainting, and death—these are to be understood as the first [stage], in their respective order. || 22 ||
The gazing with respect and the delight of the eyes are highly praised:
"O King Manu, she looked at you with sidelong glances that stole away the pride from the gait of intoxicated female bees emerging from the corners of half-blown lotuses;
those glances were languid with modesty and possessed hundreds of graceful expressions."
Attachment of the mind arises through constant reflection on remedies and the like, just as [in the previous case]. || 23 ||
O King Manu, she was unable to paint you out of shame;
having reflected for a long time in my presence,
she painted instead two lotuses, two elephant trunks, the sky, and a door-panel.
"A pair of lotuses, and then the moon.
Thus is described the mental resolve (*saṅkalpa*) as the pervasion of the beloved through desires:
"With eyes closed, the forehead region disheveled by locks of hair, cheeks perspiring, and lovely with the quivering of the lower lip..."
Placing her face upon his hand, O King, she finds delight in her desires through the excellence of his touch.
Just as wakefulness arises from the constant anxiety of not attaining one's beloved: || 24 ||

O King of my heart, that friend of mine knows no difference between the full moon and the sun, nor does she feel any distinction between sleep and wakefulness, due to the showers of arrows born from the God of Love.
"O son of the Lord of Lakṣmī,

for this fawn-eyed woman who is devoted to you, night and day have become wretched due to her separation from you; because she has not obtained you, her body has become emaciated by the fever of desire, just as [the body] wastes away."
"O Lord of my heart, her body emaciated by the fever of love,
she makes her own thinness appear truly beautiful as she strives to find a place within your lovely heart."
Intolerance toward other meanings is, for example, aversion toward the subject matter. || 25 ||
Hearing the buzzing of the swarm of bees, the innocent girl becomes afraid;
looking at her face, she abandons the mirror;
and though afflicted by the pain of love, she does not even sigh softly.

"O King Cupid, have the breezes from the Malaya mountains begun to blow gently out of fear of you— the breeze that causes the abandonment of pride, the destruction of shame, and the disregard for dignity?"
Intoxicated by the nectar of honey, the bees hum;
O Lord of my land, the female swan, fearing the fall of Love’s arrows, abandons her pride and no longer resorts to the vehicle of the male swan.
Insanity, due to the derangement of the mind, is called delusion, as follows.
"Having gently entreated the mango tree, saying, 'Come, take hold of this branch with its swaying sprouts,' she,
O King Manmatha, terrifying by your embrace of her youth, is unable to shed the tears from her eyes out of anger. Thus,
due to the impairment of her senses, she repeatedly fell into a swoon, which is the loss of consciousness.

O King of my mind, my innocent friend repeatedly seeks a swoon to conceal the pain caused by the arrows of Love; for she desires to avoid discernment, as it would reveal the specific nature of her suffering.
Closing her eyes, she does not accept [the medicine], for in a moment death from losing her life would be like the death that comes from the loss of her beloved. || 27 ||

"O King of my heart, if there were some ancient merit remaining here, then Cupid would not lead this curly-haired woman— who is devoted out of compassion— to such a tenth stage [of death] even with so much time, had she been able to ascend your lap without hesitation.
Laughter itself, when nourished by its determinants (*vibhāva*) and other factors, attains the state of the comic (*hāsya*).
The *ālambana* (objective basis) is the character of the Vidūṣaka and others; the emotion (*bhāva*) is the comic sentiment (*hāsyarasa*). Thus [ends verse 28].

Intoxicated by the drinking of honey-wine, she placed her hand— purified by constant contact with the broom and cleansed by the waters of many sacred fords— upon my head as if it were a purificatory blade of grass.
"Fie upon his pride here, for it leads only to contempt!
The excitants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*) are the transformations of the body's form resulting from that emotion;
the ensuants (*anubhāva*) are proclaimed to be the expansion of the eyes and other such expressions of the experiencer. (29)
Tears, change of complexion, change of voice, and so forth are known as the *sāttvika* [emotions].
In this context, emotions such as laughter and tears are considered *sañcārī* (transitory) states.
The sentiment of humor (hāsya-rasa) is considered to be threefold according to the distinctions of superior and so forth;
here, the two [lower] types of superior humor have smiling (smita) and laughing (hasita) as their attendant emotions (anubhāva).

The first is the blooming smile (vikāsigaṇḍa), the next is that in which the teeth are slightly visible; the middle one is the laughing smile (vihasita), and the next is the mocking smile (upahasita). || 32 ||
The first [type of laughter] is considered to be a gentle sound with a slight shaking of the head;
the inferior [types] are considered to be the derisive laugh and the excessive laugh.
The second [type] is preceded by shaking the head and shedding tears, with the limbs cast about;
grief itself, when nourished by the determinants (vibhāvas) and other factors, attains the state of the pathetic sentiment (karuṇa). || 34 ||
Compassion is also considered to be of two kinds due to the loss of what is desired or the attainment of what is undesired;
for example, as when a kinsman who has perished, or one who is joined with the undesired, serves as the objective support.
"O Lord, who would offer you nectar today, and how? You have now lost your eyesight.
Alas! How could one devoid of compassion forcibly [take it from you]?"
Yama seized Yaṣṭimadhū, who was held fast by her staff.
"Being led away by the cruel servants of the king's son along a path crowded with travelers, his own arms were bound behind him with cords."
"Listen! Out of passionlessness, this lily-born [Kamala], born of the family of the Lotus-born [Brahmā] and timid of soul, is being led away to be slain.
The excitants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*) are the wailing of one's own kin and so forth.
The manifestations (anubhāvas), however, are sighing, lamentation, weeping, and so forth. || 36 ||
The *sāttvika* [emotions], headed by paralysis, shedding tears, and loss of voice, are clearly manifested here;
as are epilepsy, dejection, death, lassitude, and agitation. (37)

Despondency, dullness, madness, anxiety, and other such transitory states [arise from it]; and it is anger itself, when nourished by its determinants (vibhāvas) and other factors, that attains the state of the Furious sentiment (raudra-rasa).
Furthermore, the fierce type is also twofold, arising from both envy and hatred, as follows:
"From birth a celibate student, his triumphal inscription of victory over the earth is the series of scars from the striking of the bowstring upon his massive, pillar-like arms;
crushing the arrows against his chest-plate, hardened by the calluses of wounds from the bow and missiles—"
The son of Jamadagni, eager for the hunt of wild elephants in the forest of the assembly of kings, has arrived.
"By you, who are like beasts among men, devoid of all restraint and with weapons raised, this heinous crime was committed, or approved, or witnessed."
"Together with Naraka’s enemy, along with Bhīma and Kirīṭin, I shall offer a sacrifice to the quarters with their marrow, blood, fat, and flesh.
The two objective excitants (ālambana-vibhāva) are the objects of envy and hatred. (39)

The excitants (uddīpanavibhāvas) are its language, gestures, and so forth; the consequents (anubhāvas) are the knitting of the brows, the reddening of the eyes, the quivering of the lips, and so on. || 40 ||
Perspiration, change of color, loss of voice, and so forth are considered the *sāttvika* [emotions];
envy, indignation, ferocity, pride, intoxication, and so forth are the *vyabhicārin* (transitory) states. (41)
Enthusiasm, when nourished by the determinants (vibhāva) and other factors, becomes the heroic sentiment (vīrarasa);
it is threefold, as in the case of the hero of generosity, the hero of compassion, and the hero of battle. || 42 ||
The earth, with its four boundaries demarcated by the trunks of the elephants of the quarters, is being conquered;
and even as we speak of it as already conquered, our hair stands on end—behold! It is now being bestowed upon a Brahmin. What more can be said? Homage to that Rāma!
"Since this wonder appeared from that very source, it has set back into that same place.
Even now, blood still flows from the openings of my veins, and there is still flesh in my body;
yet I do not see any end to my hunger."
"O Garuḍa, why have you desisted from eating?
O horses, cast away this fear; you have already crushed the temples of Indra’s elephant. These arrows now falling upon your bodies feel only the greatest shame."
"O Saumitri, stay back; you are indeed no vessel for my wrath. Surely I am Meghanāda, who seeks Rāma—that one who restrained the ocean by the mere play of a slight frown.
In the first case, he is called a worthy recipient; in the second, a wretched man.
The enemy is to be understood in the third; therein, the excitants (uddīpana) follow in sequence. (43)

Praise of generosity, words of compassion for the distressed, and the sounds of battle drums are, respectively, his manifestations for the purpose of bestowing grace, for the sake of wealth, and for the purpose of gathering an army. (44)

In this context, the sattvic [manifestations] such as horripilation (pulaka) and so forth, as well as the transitory emotions (sañcārin) such as pride, joy, indignation, and fortitude, should be understood according to their appropriate application. || 45 ||
The sentiment of fear (bhayānaka-rasa) arises precisely from the manifestation of fear and its causes, as for example:
"O lotus-eyed one, cover your body, which possesses a flickering luster, with this blue garment."
"Thus do your enemies, hidden in mountain caves, cry out upon seeing the destruction of darkness.
Enemies, tigers, serpents, and the like, are the *ālambana-vibhāvas* (the objective determinants). (46)
In this context, the excitants (uddīpanavibhāvas) would be its thundering and so forth;
the ensuants (anubhāvas), however, are such as change of color, trembling, perspiration, and the like. || 47 ||
These very sattvic states are eightfold there with clearly defined characteristics;
the transitory states (sañcārins) include delusion, dejection, fear, agitation, and so forth. (48)
Disgust itself, when brought to the state of the aesthetic sentiment of the loathsome (bībhatsa) through the determinants (vibhāva) and other factors, becomes twofold:
one arising from the sight of the loathsome, and the other from dispassion (vairāgya), as follows. || 49 ||
By the king of Vaṅga, who was endowed with valor, his enemies were driven out;
he issued commands at every crossroads and every monastery regarding those new Kāpālikas who,
touching festering wounds, quickly drove away the flies.
They gather together the scattered fragments of vegetables from their alms-meals.
What son of noble family would kiss the sprout-like lip of a courtesan, even though it be sweet, when it is but a spittoon for spies, rogues, thieves, servants, jesters, and actors?

"May that very God, the destroyer of Madana, who bears his beloved on half his body and the moon upon his head, purify you."
Furthermore, the meaning of words such as "ca" (and), "vai" (indeed), and so forth, is not [independently] perceived. || 8 ||
Even that which is prescribed by tradition is not respected if it is not employed by poets.
"Since this man of cruel conduct is perceived in every way [as such], I think he must be a *piśāca* or even a *rākṣasa* by destiny (*daivata*).
This word *daivata*, however, is not used by poets in reference to a male being. (9)
That by which an improper meaning is illuminated through a word is called *aślīla* (the indecorous);
it is of three kinds because it manifests disgust, inauspiciousness, or shame, as follows: || 10 ||
Struck by a lotus in play, his lip bitten without hesitation by another woman,
he stood with eyes closed as if his sight were offended by the filaments; she,
the charming one, stood before him, fanning him with her bud-like face.

"Whether out of delusion or through deceit, she was incessantly kissed by him without even a bow. Here, [the phrase] "giving breath with her mouth" is loathsome. [The verse continues: "Shattered by the gentle breeze due to the death of my beloved..."
"Today this peacock has become peerless, with its plumage thick and radiant;
for whom could it captivate, were it not for the tresses of that fair-haired woman— now loosened by passion and adorned with flowers?"
This phrase, "due to the destruction of my beloved," is inauspicious.
"Who else could withstand the furrowed brow of that wise man, whose means for success is so great as not to be seen in anyone else?
Here, this word *sādhana* is considered to cause the arising of shame.
That which is fit for villagers is "village-like" (grāmya), just as that which is censured by city-dwellers [is so called]. (12)
"Your face, which has transferred its luster to the beloved of the night (the moon) during the full moon,
and your waist, which possesses the beauty of a plate of refined gold, captivate the mind.
Here, the word *kaṭi* (waist) is censured because it denotes a private part of the body.
That which, due to a lack of capacity, indicates a remote meaning is of interpretable meaning (neyārtha), as for example: || 13 ||
"O slender one, your face, which is dear to the autumn night shining with the full moon, makes itself a recipient of a slap."
In this context, the word "capeṭa" (slap) does not denote victory by implication;
rather, that very [word] would be of improper meaning for one whose referent is inappropriate, as in the following example. || 14 ||
That state which is attained only after a long time by ascetics through diligent effort, and which is sought even by those engaged in sacrificial rites—
those of noble mind go to that destination swiftly.
"In the Horse Sacrifice of battle, they have become sacrificial animals.
Here, the word *paśu* (animal), though appropriate, reveals cowardice in the hero.
Furthermore, as it were, it suggests something other than the intended meaning and is ambiguous, as follows: || 15 ||

"May your lordship, having placed upon his ear the venerable succession of blessings for the glory of victory in the final struggle, show compassion. Here, the word *vandyām* (venerable) [is used] in the sense of both "captured" (*bandīkṛta*) and "to be saluted" (*namasya*).
Just as an afflicted word may indicate a meaning that is obscured. || 16 ||
"O King, your conduct shines exceedingly, resembling that which is illuminated by the rising light born from the eye of Atri.
Here, the one born from the eye of Atri is the Moon; [the conduct resembles] the rising of its light.
The phrase "like the withered night-lotuses" indicates defilement due to obstruction. || 17 ||
That by which a portion of the subject matter is touched upon primarily, as for example:
"She repeatedly let her girdle of saffron filaments, which had slipped from her hips, hang down."
"She was made into a [quiver-like] deposit by Smara, who knows the proper place, like a second bowstring for his bow.
Here, the element to be predicated (vidheyāṃśa) is primarily indicated by the accusative case ending. (18)
One who performs desired and non-evil actions is like one who produces a contrary cognition.
"His conduct is as skillful as the rays of the moon;
he alone is a friend in times of adversity—how can we possibly describe him?
This is said when the intended meaning is that he is a friend even without any self-interest. (19)
In the phrase "a friend in misfortune," another meaning, which is contradictory, is perceived;
this is considered an "unintelligible" (apratīta) word, as its meaning is established solely by technical treatises. (20)
"For one who possesses the state of having destroyed the latent tendencies (*āśaya*) by means of the great light of perfect knowledge (*samyagjñāna*),
even this [action] being performed would not become a bond of karma.
Here, the word *āśaya* has the meaning of "latent impression" (*vāsanā*) and is established by scriptural authority (*āgama*).
I shall state the faults regarding individual parts of words as appropriate. || 21 ||

"Enough with this fickleness! Because of its being like a dream or an illusion, and because of the bitterness of its ultimate transformation, we have reflected upon the reality of union with a woman a hundred times; yet even so, the inner self does not forget the deer-eyed one.
Here, due to the excessive use of the suffix *tva*, it is said to be harsh to the ear (*śrutikaṭu*).
"First, her eyes have their forms smeared with a mass of collyrium; then, they are scorched by the spreading fire of separation fanned by the wind of her sighs.
Now, the deer-eyed woman performs, at will, the act of mixing the tears of the god whose mind is love with the water of her own tears—like the preparation of a medicinal drink for hunters.
In this case, the plurality of "eyes" would be meaningless, as it refers to the eyes of a single woman. (22)
Because the fruit of the action does not accrue to the agent, the *ātmanepada* suffix is used after the root *kṛ*.

"He who is purified by bathing together at the sacred fords on the banks of the celestial river, and by the study and recitation of the scriptures—he who has acquired a noble birth and a reputation for magnanimity—falls within the sight of only a rare individual.
Here, in the word *pūya* ("pus"), an indecorous meaning of loathing is perceived. (23)

"Salutation to that Lord of the Gaṇas, who is worshipped even by the gods for the sake of accomplishing desired aims, and who cuts asunder all obstacles. Herein, in the word *preta*, an inauspicious and vulgar meaning is perceived.
"In what action does his capacity not excel?
Therefore, let this salutation with joined palms be offered here to him who walks the path of the virtuous.
[In the phrase] "one who formerly walked as a rogue," there is a doubt as to whether he was a rogue or one walking virtuously.
"What is being said of this great jewel upon the garland of the crowns of kings—that whose splendor is perceived [only] by the arrows of his speech?
Here, the word *vacaḥ* (speech) is used to indicate the word *gīḥ* (song); thus, it is a case of non-expressive usage (*avācaka*). (24)

That which has an offensive sound, where the *visarga* is damaged or lost, where there is a hiatus (*visandhi*) or a defective meter (*hatavṛtta*), where words are deficient, redundant, or repeated; where the excellence [of the style] declines, or where what was concluded is resumed again;

where there is a single word for two meanings (*arthāntaraikavācaka*), where the intended connection is not realized (*abhavanmatayoga*), or where the expressed meaning is left unstated (*anabhihitavācya*). || 25 ||
A compound with misplaced words, a confused compound, an interrupted compound, and one that contradicts established usage. || 26 ||
Broken sequence, lack of sequence, non-appositional word-meaning, and likewise the loss of rasa—
these, as well as the irrelevant subject matter, are defects that occur in sentences.
This [work] has an unattractive appearance, for its syllables do not conform to the aesthetic flavor (rasa) in that manner. || 27 ||
"O sweet-voiced one! With unflagging longing, fill me to my throat;
O lady with the neck of a conch, place me for a moment upon your neck and deliver me, who am a suppliant at your throat.
In the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) sentiment, hard consonants such as *ṭa* and others are not favorable here.
When the *ut* or *aut* [sandhi] has been applied, if the *visarjanīya* should be elided, they declare that sentence to be defective, as it contains a corrupted or elided *visarjanīya*. || 28 ||
"The king here is wise, disciplined, skillful, of noble form, and fearless;
his servants are exultant in their strength, devoted, and distinguished by their intelligence.
In the first half of this verse, the *visarga* (the final *s*) undergoes elision (*upahatatā*), while in the subsequent [half], it is subject to elision (*luptatva*) by the following vowel.
Deformity, disjunction, vulgarity, and harshness of euphonic combination (saṃdhi) [are defects]. || 29 ||
Wise men describe defects as being of various kinds according to their sequence,
as follows: "O King, your deeds shine forth,
which possess the luster of the moon even within the depths of the netherworld."
"Exerting the strength of your intellect and arms beyond measure and following established custom, you shine forth having attained the fullness of victory.
Yet, even if a single fault is committed here once, if it is repeated, deformity arises. (30)
"Then, like the moon rising from the high eastern mountain, the noble and captivating splendor arose;
indeed, within his own lineage, he of exalted and lovely luster shone like a priceless pearl.
Even though this [example] has been provided, the fault of *viśleṣa* (separation of words) should be understood as occurring repeatedly.
"The beloved woman of the Guhyakas, who comes to you at night while you are practicing your lore—how can your forest be so delicate?
Here, those possessed of discernment should recognize the fault of indecorousness (*aślīlatva*) in the euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*). (31)
"This row of trees here is vast; its beautiful state persists in every season.
It is not possible to pass through here—bend your head slightly.
In this instance, the harshness of the *sandhi* (euphonic junction) is described as a defect occurring once due to its being *kliṣṭa* (obscure).
The lack of conformity [to the rules] regarding the heavy and light syllables occurs where there is deficiency or excess.
They say that [a verse] has its meter and syntax broken and its rhythmic structure destroyed, as for example:
"By Kāma, all five arrows were discharged at the deer-eyed women"— this is an instance of improper weight (*ayathāgurutva*).

"The sharp arrows of Love fall upon the fair-eyed women"— this is an example of *ayathālaghutva* (inappropriate lightness). "The cool rays of the moon touch [her]"— this is an example of *ūnavarṇatā* (deficiency of syllables).
"His [lips] are like fresh sprouts"—this contains an extra syllable. (33)
The breaking of the pause (yati) at the end of a foot or in the middle of one constitutes a defect here, as in this example:
"Born in the great lineage of Āditya, this king, Dhanakīrti,
who is adorned with abundant compassion and is affectionate toward those of many virtues, triumphs upon the earth."
They consider that word by the absence of which a sentence becomes deficient to be a "deficient word" (*nyūnapada*), as for example: || 34 ||
Having seen her in such a state in the assembly of kings— the daughter of Pañcāla who had dwelt for a long time in the forest with hunters, wearing bark garments,
and now staying in the residence of Virāṭa, concealed by engaging in unsuitable tasks—
"The Guru feels distress; even now he does not show favor toward the Kurus while I am thus afflicted.
Here, because the substantive (*viśeṣya*) "by us" is absent, the sentence is stated as deficient.

Since it is complete even in the absence of that [substantive], there is a redundant word (*adhikapada*) here, as follows: [Verse 35] The moon, having ascended the peak of the eastern mountain, is being embraced by the eastern quarter, while the lotuses, their faces turned away, are being kissed by bees. In this verse, the word *mukhaiḥ* ("by faces") is redundant, for the meaning is already established by the word *ambujaiḥ* ("by lotuses"). Furthermore, the word *parāṅmukhaiḥ* ("with faces turned away") is also superfluous, since the bees do not kiss the lotuses with their own mouths. Moreover, the word *purogiriśikharaṃ* ("the peak of the eastern mountain") is unnecessary, because the moon’s ascent of the eastern mountain is well known. Finally, the word *prācīmukhī* ("facing the east") is redundant, as the direction is already indicated by the word *prācyā* ("by the eastern [quarter]"). Thus, these words are considered superfluous. However, if they were used to provide specific detail, they would not be faults. For example: [Verse 36] The moon, having ascended the peak of the eastern mountain, is being embraced by the eastern quarter, while the lotuses, their faces turned away, are being kissed by bees. In this case, the word *mukhaiḥ* is employed to indicate that the bees are kissing the lotuses from the front, and the word *parāṅmukhaiḥ* is used to show that the bees are kissing the lotuses from behind. Therefore, these words are not faulty. Likewise, the word *purogiriśikharaṃ* is used to distinguish this from the western mountain, and the word *prācīmukhī* is used to distinguish this from the southern quarter. Consequently, when used for such specific qualification, these words are not considered superfluous. However, if one were to say: [Verse 37] The moon, having ascended the peak of the eastern mountain, is being embraced by the eastern quarter, while the lotuses, their faces turned away, are being kissed by bees. In this instance, the word *mukhaiḥ* is indeed redundant, as the meaning is already conveyed by the word *ambujaiḥ*. Furthermore, the word *parāṅmukhaiḥ* is also superfluous, because the bees do not kiss the lotuses with their own mouths. Moreover, the word *purogiriśikharaṃ* is unnecessary, since the moon’s ascent of the eastern mountain is well known. And the word *prācīmukhī* is redundant, as the direction is already indicated by the word *prācyā*. Thus, these words are considered superfluous. However, if they were used to provide specific detail, they would not be faults. For example: [Verse 38] The moon, having ascended the peak of the eastern mountain, is being embraced by the eastern quarter, while the lotuses, their faces turned away, are being kissed by bees. In this case, the word *mukhaiḥ* is employed to indicate that the bees are kissing the lotuses from the front, and the word *parāṅmukhaiḥ* is used to show that the bees are kissing the lotuses from behind. Therefore, these words are not faulty. Likewise, the word *purogiriśikharaṃ* is used to distinguish this from the western mountain, and the word *prācīmukhī* is used to distinguish this from the southern quarter. Consequently, when used for such specific qualification, these words are not considered superfluous. However, if one were to say: [Verse 39] The moon, having ascended the peak of the eastern mountain, is being embraced by the eastern quarter, while the lotuses, their faces turned away, are being kissed by bees. In this instance, the word *mukhaiḥ* is indeed redundant, as the meaning is already conveyed by the word *ambujaiḥ*. Furthermore, the word *parāṅmukhai
Stainless like the form of crystal, having thoroughly reflected upon the principles of the sharp sciences,
and possessing a method of expression that is both consistent and coherent.
"That is some extraordinary phenomenon, like the setting and rising of rival stars.
Here, even without a sentence, the meaning becomes complete through the word *ākṛti* (form/appearance).
As for the fault of the "repeated word" (*kathitapada*), it occurs when there is merely the utterance of a word that has already been stated, as follows: [36]
O fair-limbed one! Tell me, whose cheeks— rendered exceedingly pale by the pressure of the broad bed and closed by the play of sleep—
clearly manifest [the state of passion]?

[This is] the coronation of the heir-apparent to the playful sovereignty of the Lord of Remembrance (Smara). Regarding the word *līlā*, which was previously mentioned, it is stated here once again as *līlā*.
They declare that in this [context], excellence falls away from its highest state, just as [they describe it]. 37.
Which fierce boar, with its snout making a ghur-ghur sound, would grunt where?
Which elephant is not intent on making which lotus pond devoid of lotuses? And which forest buffaloes would not uproot which forests? For [all are present].
"The lion, having made his dwelling through the playful affection of the lioness, remains [there].
In this instance, the poet mentions the elephants after having already mentioned the superior buffaloes;
furthermore, they say that when a statement is completed and then begun again, it is called *samāptapunarātta* (resuming what was finished), as for example: || 38 ||
The tinkling of the bow of Love, the cry of the cuckoos of amorous play, the humming of the bees that are the clusters of passion, the call of the playful female cakora birds,
and the sound of bracelets slipping from the tossing arms of the slender maiden as she discards her bodice— [all these constitute the music of love].
"May the sound of the flute, resonating with the melody of youth, spread love for you.
Here, although the meaning has already been concluded, it is taken up again at the end of the final quarter-verse.
As for *arthāntaraikavācaka* (a single expressive word referring to another meaning), it is as follows: || 39 ||
"Walk with gentle steps; the ground is covered with darbha grass;
place the hem of your garment upon your head, for the heat is fierce.
Thus spoke the daughter of Janaka with eyes filled with tears.
On the road, she was gazed upon by the wives of travelers and instructed by them:

"In this [verse], the word *tat* (that) is the cause; [the fault lies] in the phrase 'arrange the edge of the garment upon your head,' where the connection of the intended meaning is absent because the word has become subordinate within the compound. (40)
One does not attain yoga for its intended purpose through other primary factors as one does through these:
"We four are the officiating priests, the Blessed Lord Hari is the preceptor of the rite,
the king is the patron consecrated for the sacrifice of battle, and his queen has taken her vow."
"The Kauravas are the sacrificial animals; the pacification of the suffering caused by the humiliation of their beloved is the fruit;
the drum of abundant fame resounds for the invitation of the kings.
Here, the compound word *saṅgrāmādhvara* (the sacrifice of battle) incurs the status of a fault. (41)
This is an example of the "unexpressed" (anabhihitavācya), wherein that which ought not to be said has been stated, as for instance: "In you, who are naturally delighted, who speak kindly,
and whose mind is averse to breaking a friend's affection..."
"O proud one, what speck of an offense do you see in me that you abandon your servant?
In this case, the phrase "you see even a speck of an offense" must necessarily be stated. (42)
"An ill-placed word" is that where a word stands in an inappropriate place, as for example:

"A seal-mark upon the surface of her cheek, left within the midst of sleep by the crescent moon on the blue-throated Lord’s shoulder hanging down from his matted locks loosened by the grasping of her hair in play."

"May that curved, copper-hued [line] protect you, which was wiped away by Pārvatī with her sprout-like hand when she was put to shame by the playful smile of her friends, who suspected it to be the mark of a fingernail.
The phrase "curved, copper-hued" should have been stated before "the mark of a fingernail," and so forth. (43)
*Asthānasthasamāsa* (misplaced compound) refers to that which possesses a compound in an inappropriate place, as for example:
"Even now, this pride (*māna*)— as if red with anger, exclaiming 'Fie!'— desires to remain in the hearts of women, which are difficult to traverse due to the mountain-fortresses of their breasts."
"Extending its rays far and wide as it rises, this moon instantly draws forth the sword-like rows of bees emerging from the cups of the blooming night-lotuses.
In this instance of angry speech, no compound has been formed; however, this is the case only in the speech of a poet.
Confused (saṅkīrṇa) is that [type of sentence] where the words of one sentence occur within another, as for example:
"Why do you not look at this anger at my feet, which possesses many virtues? Take it!
Indeed, release from your neck this lord of your heart, who is the very embodiment of the darkness of your mind!"
In this case, there is a mutual interpenetration of the words and sentences of the various [verses], which is more clearly evident. || 45 ||

Defilement (*kliṣṭatva*) occurs within a single sentence; however, when there are many sentences, it becomes "mixed" (*saṅkīrṇa*). Another [type of defect] is the "embryonic" (*garbhita*), where another sentence exists in the middle of a single sentence. (46)

"Association with wicked people who delight in harming others—this I tell you as the truth: it should never be practiced. In this sentence, which stands among other sentences, I tell you the truth: "I tell you the truth."
In this regard, a word that is devoid of conventional renown is said to be endowed with renown, as follows: || 47 ||

"This unprecedented roar of the ocean of battle today has repeatedly imitated the fierce thundering of the Puṣkalāvarta clouds agitated by the winds of the great dissolution; it is terrifying to the ear and has filled the hollows between heaven and earth. The word *rava* (roar) is a specific modifier of sound that is well-known to apply to sound in general.
That in which there is a breaking of the form commenced is called "broken sequence" (bhagnaprakrama). || 48 ||
That [meaning] is manifested through various divisions, primarily by means of roots (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*), as follows in sequence:
"When the Lord of Night had gone to his setting by the decree of destiny, alas, the night too has departed.
For noble women, there is indeed nothing more auspicious than a state consistent with their circumstances."
When "gone" (gata) was intended [as the subject], the root "to go" (yāta) is used here in a manner that involves a formal deviation (bhaṅga). || 49 ||
Whether to attain fame, or out of a desire for pleasure,
or to transcend the ranks of ordinary men—
for those who are free from worldly longing yet devoted to diligent effort, [this path exists].
"Success approaches as if eager to sit upon one's lap.
Here, the subversion of the causal factor (*pratyayabhaṅga*)—namely, the desire for pleasure—should be understood by discerning it.
Other such subversions of the causal factor should also be known here, though they are not elaborated upon. || 50 ||
Where a specific sequence is prescribed, they recite the statement that it is "out of order," as for example:
"May Viṣṇu, the three-eyed Śiva, and the lotus-born Brahmā— regarded as the causes of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the worlds— protect you."
Although one should say "Parameṣṭhin, Hari, Hara," the order of the planets is reversed here.
An example where the meaning of the word *amata* (unintended) consists precisely in stating a sense contrary to the subject at hand is as follows:
"Struck in the heart by the unbearable arrow of Rāma, the god of love, the night-stalker woman..."
"Smeared with fragrant blood as if with sandalwood paste, she went to the abode of the Lord of Life.
In this context, which is characterized by a [tragic] sentiment, the description of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) is employed in a manner that is contradictory. (52)
Where there is no rasa in a sentence, they declare it to be devoid of rasa, as for example:
"The one-tailed, four-footed, humped animal with a long dewlap—
the ox, the offspring of the cow— eats fodder at his ease."
Even the poetic figure *jāti* (natural description), because it lacks aesthetic flavor (*nīrasatva*), is not an ornament for this [poem], but rather constitutes a defect. || 53 ||
This is Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Indirect Description), which by effort brings about the praise of something not directly under discussion, as for example:
"This Hanumān has leaped across the salt ocean with his foot— dark as the tamāla tree, exceedingly clear, and overflowing with foam."
In this context, the description of qualities such as dark complexion would not be useful there. || 54 ||
The meaning may be undeveloped, difficult, contradictory, redundant, of bad order, vulgar, doubtful, groundless, or contrary to common usage and science. (55)
Futile, that which involves the reversal of specific and non-specific rules along with their observances;
that which is expectant, contradictory to what was stated, arrogant, retracted, or vulgar.
Those [faults] which are distinct from the primary and secondary [meanings], and which cease upon the completion of the injunction and its restatement, would be defects of meaning. || 56 ||
When the stated qualifiers do not serve to nourish the qualificand because their result is not perceived, that is considered "un-nourished meaning" (apuṣṭārtha), as for example: [57]
"Victorious is the Sun, who brings laughter to the lotus-pool whose fragrance is wafted by the breeze, and who has abandoned the joy of rest while traversing the vast expanse of the sky.
The victory of the Sun does not belong to one who possesses the joy of being free from rest.
It is difficult and to be understood only with great effort, as it is presented here through a concise summary of terminology.
"Is it perhaps the quality of causing the wheel to spin that belongs to the potter's stick, produced by its own cause, which—
residing in her lofty breasts— spreads a whirling illusion of a flood of light?
The meaning here is not understood through sheer force, as it is obscured by extreme distance."
Just as in a sentence, excellence belongs only to that which is not disregarded; otherwise, it would be contradicted. || 59 ||
In this world, there are indeed those victorious things— such as the crescent of the new moon and others— which are naturally sweet and delight the mind;
yet for me, it is she who has become the moonlight for my eyes in this world.
In this world, that alone is a great festival which comes within the range of the eyes.
Here, disregarding the crescent moon and such, the moonlight alone is praised;
this is considered a tautology (punarukta), just as a single meaning expressed twice is deemed redundant.

"While this commander-in-chief, my father and the preceptor of all masters of archery, stands here like the submarine fire within the ocean of the enemy forces licked by the flames of his weapons—O Karṇa, enough with your agitation! Go, Kṛpa! Abandon your fear of the son of Hṛdika in battle!"
"When our father bears the burden of battle with his bow as his only companion, what room is there for fear?
Here, the repetition of meaning in the two *samā* compounds is well-known.
As for the inversion of meanings that ought to be stated, that is "bad order" (*duṣkrama*), as in: (61) [Example follows].
"O jewel among kings! O you whose festival of giving is renowned for its freedom from stinginess!
Bestow upon me either a horse or an elephant languid with rut.
Here, the mention of the elephant (*mātaṅga*) should have been made first; let that be understood.
That meaning which is uttered by those who are shameless is called "vulgar," as for example: || 62 ||
"I bow to the temple of Love belonging to the deer-eyed women, which resembles the hoof of a deer placed upon a muddy surface and is devoid of hair.
Here, the vulgarity of the meaning is clearly perceived as being well-known.
An object perceived in two ways is "doubtful" because of the lack of a definitive conclusion, as for example: [53]
"O noble ones, casting aside stinginess and considering the matter at hand, please speak this with due propriety:
Are the slopes of mountains to be enjoyed, or rather the hips of playful women smiling with passion?
Whether the speaker here be dispassionate or impassioned, let there be a definitive conclusion."
Just as it is said where an effect is asserted to exist without a cause, being causeless. 64.

"O Weapon! You were taken up by him because of his power—there was indeed no one who was not within his reach—even though you were unsuitable for him out of fear of humiliation. Yet, you have been abandoned by him due to grief for his son, and not out of fear; therefore, I too shall release you, so that well-being be yours.
In the phrase "I too shall release," there is no further reason [for the release] of the weapon.
That which is contradicted by common consensus is what is unknown to the world, as for example: || 65 ||
"Tell me, O lotus-eyed one who terrifies her enemies, who told you this, that you should indeed entertain the notion that this is a girdle of gold?
This is rather the supreme weapon of the God of Love for the conquest of those difficult to subdue."
"Out of affection for you, the discus has been placed at the base of your lotus-hand.
Here, the discus is said to be the weapon of the Mind-born (Kāma), though it is not well-known [in that sense].
It is stated to be contrary to established knowledge (*vidyā*) because it contradicts the *Smṛtis* and other authorities, as follows: [66]
Having always bathed at midnight, the wise man expounds and listens to various kinds of scriptures throughout the entire day.
Bathing at night without an eclipse is censured by the Vedas;
for it is like rendering useless that which is praiseworthy by bringing about its futility. || 67 ||
What is gained from attaining fortunes that grant all desires?
What is gained from placing one's foot upon the heads of enemies?
What is gained from fully satisfying one's loved ones with riches?
"What is gained by embodied beings remaining in their bodies for an eon?"—here, the uselessness of the objects [of desire] alone is stated, not their purpose.

That which is a restriction regarding an inappropriate object would be *saniyama* (restriction), as in the following example: 68. "That which is a restriction regarding an inappropriate object would be *saniyama*.
